    #23466. Latest Update: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3808 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
    • Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
    • Recent findings suggest that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

    Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

    Recent findings suggest that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

    Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

    We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

    It has been revealed that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

    Recent findings suggest that for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

    Industry observers note that RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

    In a recent development, this section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

    In a recent development, each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

    Recent findings suggest that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

    It has been revealed that A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

    In a recent development, each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

    In a recent development, 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

    According to recent reports, A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

    Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

    Recent findings suggest that qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

    This example indicates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

    In a recent development, the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

    According to recent reports, each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

    It has been revealed that the figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

    Sources indicate that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below reveals what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

    We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

    For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

    It has been revealed that to obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

    The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which demonstrated that 0.1 worked best).

    We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

    Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below highlights the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

    As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

    Industry observers note that the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

    Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

    We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

    The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

    Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

    In a recent development, we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

    We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each enhancement below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

    Sources indicate that the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

    Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

    It has been revealed that "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

    With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

    In a recent development, despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

    Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

    The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

    The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

    This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

    Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

    Sources indicate that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

    On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

    This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

    According to recent reports, we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

    Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

    For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

    For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

    All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

    The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

    To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

    Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

    What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

    We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

    Sources indicate that results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

    Recent findings suggest that we appreciate the feedback from the consumers and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

    Recent findings suggest that this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

    According to recent reports, this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

    Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

    In a recent development, however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

    Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

    In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

    Recent findings suggest that we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

    Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

    #23463. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2388 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model.
    • Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
    • Sources indicate that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

    Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

    Sources indicate that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

    This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

    Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

    Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

    Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

    Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

    In a recent development, in addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

    Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

    Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

    In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

    We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

    You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

    To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

    Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

    Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

    Recent findings suggest that in this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

    If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

    Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

    For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

    Recent findings suggest that here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

    Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

    One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

    SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

    We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

    We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

    MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

    We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

    The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

    Over the Still Sea (Qwen 3.8 27B).

    According to recent reports, build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

    Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889).

    According to recent reports, we gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

    Sources indicate that inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

    According to recent reports, in this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

    Recent findings suggest that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness.     #23459. I turned my own portfolio into an IDE-style site, and what I would change

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1345 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    I turned my own portfolio into an IDE-style site, and what I would change

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that my portfolio used to look like every other developer portfolio.
    • An editor window has a shape most developers read without thinking.
    • My portfolio maps onto that shape with no forcing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that my portfolio used to look like every other developer portfolio. A large name at the top, a short line about building websites, a grid of project cards, and a contact form at the bottom. It was accurate and it was forgettable, including to me. I spend most of my working day inside a code editor, so last year I rebuilt the site to look like one. The live version runs at mehedimansurrafi.online, and it is the site I send with every proposal now. This post covers why I chose the layout, what using it has taught me, and what I would change if I started again.

    An editor window has a shape most developers read without thinking. A file tree on the left lists everything in the project. The main area highlights one open file at a time. Tabs along the top show what else is open. A status bar at the bottom carries the small details.

    My portfolio maps onto that shape with no forcing. The file tree became the menu: home, projects, each project as its own file, about, contact, resume. Each page reads like an open file, with the project pages written the way a readme is written, what the thing does first, then the stack, then the links. The status bar carries my location, my availability, and a contact link, so they stay visible on every page without a banner shouting about them.

    According to recent reports, the honest reason is simpler than the design argument. The layout says what I do before a visitor reads a word. A clinic owner may not care, and this site is not aimed at clinic owners. It is aimed at developers and at the clients who hire developers and have learned to read a GitHub profile. For that audience, an editor is a familiar room.

    According to recent reports, I have no analytics story to tell here, and I will not invent one. What I know comes from sharing the link and watching what people open, and from testing the site myself the way a visitor would.

    Two differences stand out against my old layout. The first is that people treat the file tree as a table of contents and click it directly. On the old site, the path was scroll and hope: hero, about, projects somewhere below. Here the whole site is listed on the left from the first second, and a visitor with one question, what has he built, goes straight to the projects folder. The second difference is order. Visitors open the project files before the about page. On a normal portfolio the about section sits high and gets read early. Here the work reads first and the person reads later, which is the order I would choose for them anyway.

    According to recent reports, the cost is real too. A visitor who has never used an editor meets a busier first screen than a name and a grid. Some of the editor decoration, the line numbers and the tab shapes, is pure costume for them. I accept that cost because of who the site is for, but it is the first thing I would weigh if the audience changed.

    The file tree menu stays. It indicates the full site at a glance and it never moves, which a top navigation bar on a long page cannot do.

    It has been revealed that the project pages stay written like readme files. A fixed shape, problem, build, stack, live link, code link, means a visitor can read the second project faster than the first, because they already know where each fact sits.

    The status bar stays. Contact details that are visible on every page, without a popup or a floating button, are easier to act on than details buried at the end of one long page. Every path through the site ends one click from the contact file, and that was a deliberate choice, not an accident of the layout.

    It has been revealed that the theme switch stays. Dark is the default because the editor idea asks for it, and light is one click away, built on one set of CSS variables so both themes are the same layout wearing different colours.

    In a recent development, I started with too many files in the tree. Every small page got its own entry, and the list read like a directory dump. I merged the small pages and grouped the rest, and the tree got shorter and clearer. If I started again I would plan the tree at six to eight entries from day one.

    I dropped the fake terminal. An early version had a console panel that typed out lines about my skills. It did nothing a paragraph could not do, it slowed the page, and it was the kind of clever touch that makes a visitor watch the site perform instead of reading it. Anything in an editor layout that does not help navigation or reading is costume, and costume has to earn its place. The terminal did not.

    Sources indicate that I would also move the resume earlier. It sat low in the tree at first, grouped with the about pages. Recruiters and clients ask for a resume more than they ask for anything else on the site, so it earned a place near the top of the tree. That change came from requests, not from taste.

    According to recent reports, an editor is a wide screen tool. Shrink it to a phone and the layout fights you: the tree wants a third of the width, the tabs want a row, and the page gets what is left. My first mobile version squeezed all three in, and the text column was too narrow to read in comfort.

    The fix was to stop treating the phone layout as a smaller editor. On a small screen the sidebar closes into a menu button, the tabs go, and the page becomes a single column that reads like a document. The file names survive as the menu list, so the idea is still there, but nothing competes with the text. I check the site at 390px width, the size I use for every client build, and the rule I follow is plain: if a page needs horizontal scrolling or pinch zoom at that width, the page is not done.

    It has been revealed that this is the part of the design I would warn anyone copying it about. The desktop layout is the fun half of the work. The phone layout is where the design either becomes a real site or stays a screenshot.

    Industry observers note that other developers asked how the site was built, and the easiest honest answer was to sell the design as a template. That version is FolioForge. Turning a live Laravel platform into a template meant cutting, not adding. The live site runs on a Laravel app with an admin side, member pages, and settings. A template buyer needs none of that. They need files they can open, edit, and upload anywhere.

    So FolioForge is the static version. Plain HTML and CSS, no database, no admin panel, and a contact form that opens the visitor mail app, because a static site has no server to send mail. It keeps the parts that survived my own edits: the short file tree, the readme shaped project pages, the status bar, and the phone layout that drops the editor furniture. It drops the platform parts that only make sense on my own site.

    FolioForge is this design finished as a template. It has 6 pages, dark and light themes, and a fictional sample persona you replace with your own details. It costs $19 on Gumroad: https://mehedirafi.gumroad.com/l/folioforge.

    Recent findings suggest that I am Mehedi Mansur Rafi, a freelance Laravel developer (B.Sc. in Computer Science & Engineering). I build hospital, clinic, and small business websites, and I take website work through Fiverr: https://www.fiverr.com/mehedi__rafi. My full store is at https://mehedirafi.gumroad.com/ and my site is https://mehedimansurrafi.online.

    #23458. How to generate an accessible color palette from a single color

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1997 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    How to generate an accessible color palette from a single color

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To get an accessible palette out of a single color, what worked for me was deciding first how much contrast each step of the scale has to have against the background, and only then computing the color that meets it.
    • That's how color works in TaishoDS Core, a design system in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework, which I've just released under the MIT license: the package is @taishods/core on npm and the source is on GitHub.
    • It has been revealed that I started TaishoDS because I needed one system for my own products and for client work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To get an accessible palette out of a single color, what worked for me was deciding first how much contrast each step of the scale has to have against the background, and only then computing the color that meets it. My first attempt went the other way, spacing out lightness values, and it failed. I'll get to that below.

    That's how color works in TaishoDS Core, a design system in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework, which I've just released under the MIT license: the package is @taishods/core on npm and the source is on GitHub. I tested it with 4,096 starting colors, in light and dark mode. Across the 81,920 steps that came out, the text on each step never dropped below a contrast ratio of 4.63. WCAG's AA level asks for 4.5.

    It has been revealed that I started TaishoDS because I needed one system for my own products and for client work. Premium systems were out of my budget, and in the free ones I couldn't find the accessibility and the performance I was after in the same place. So I set one rule: quality has to be enforced by the system, not by discipline. For color, that rule means the contrast gets computed.

    The scale has ten steps, 100 to 1000. It's built like this, in this order:.

    After that, the step number means the same thing in any hue. A 500 stands about as far from the background whether it's blue or yellow, and a 600 holds light text on top in both.

    According to recent reports, the first engine did the obvious thing. It kept the hue and chroma of the brand color, threw away its lightness, and laid out ten fixed OKLCH lightness values, from 0.97 at step 100 down to 0.12 at step 1000. It looked even, and I took it for granted that contrast came out right on its own. That was only an assumption, picked up from what I'd been seeing in the tools around me.

    In a recent development, in late October I measured it with 648 colors spread around the hue wheel. For 45 of them, about 1 in 14, at least one step had text on it that fell below AA, and the worst pair, as computed, came in at 4.10. The brand color also never revealed up in its own scale: pass in #3b82f6 and you got ten blues, none of them #3b82f6.

    It has been revealed that I'm sharing this because mistakes don't embarrass me; they teach me. This one has a simple cause: WCAG contrast is computed from luminance, and two colors with the same OKLCH lightness don't have the same luminance. Evenly spaced lightness gives you a scale that looks orderly and tells you nothing about whether text will be readable.

    According to recent reports, A palette most of us know by heart makes the difference easy to see: Tailwind's. I measured the contrast on white of four of its 500 steps in version 4 (tailwindcss 4.3.5), computed from their OKLCH values. Next to them is the 500 that TaishoDS computes when you start from that same color:.

    Three of those four colors fall outside sRGB, so their number depends on the screen: on an sRGB screen, the four come out at 3.76, 3.81, 2.22 and 1.91. Tailwind is a fixed palette, which its documentation describes as carefully crafted by expert designers. Going by the numbers, my reading is that each color is tuned to look right and that the step number sorts shades from light to dark without aiming for a fixed ratio. For a palette that ships ready-made, that's a valid choice. I needed a different one because in TaishoDS the color comes from whoever uses the system, and nobody is going to hand-tune an arbitrary hex.

    It has been revealed that blue and red already had a step-500 contrast, so they stay there. Green and yellow are lighter: they sit on 400, and their 500 is a computed, darker color. When step 500 holds the starting color it keeps that color's contrast, which can run from 3.0 to 4.2; when it's a computed color, it gives 3.6. Red stays exact. Blue, green and yellow are outside sRGB: TaishoDS keeps them exact in the scale for wide-gamut screens and, in the sRGB scale, lowers their chroma to what that screen can show. That's why blue gets 3.70 and not 3.71.

    Starting from contrast isn't my idea. Adobe Leonardo generates scales from target ratios, and Material has it built into its tone scale: according to the code of its color library, a tone difference of 50 guarantees a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 or more. From Tailwind and Radix I took something else: both rotate the hue of their yellows as they get darker (Tailwind from about 102° to 54°; Radix, less). My reading is that they do it because a yellow darkened at a fixed hue ends up olive. In TaishoDS, the scale for #eab308 in light mode starts at a hue of 97° on step 100 and reaches 51° on step 1000, close to orange.

    Because dark mode is computed separately, the same color can land on different steps: #3b82f6 is 500 in light mode and 600 in dark. In both it appears exactly as you wrote it, and what changes is the scale around it.

    According to recent reports, the 4.63 from the top is the worst case in the whole sweep, and it isn't a one-off: nearly 200 scales across different hues give it, all on step 600 in dark mode. One of them is a magenta. That number is the computed one; measured on the colors once they're rounded to the 8 bits per channel a screen paints, the minimum is 4.59.

    Sources indicate that sometimes the engine moves the starting color. Between steps 500 and 600 there's a band of lightness where neither light nor dark text reaches AA on top, and no step aims there. The engine shifts with a margin: in light mode it moves any color that gives between 4.2 and 5.3 against the background, and in dark mode between 4.1 and 5.0, a zone wider than the band. If the brand color falls there, it gets shifted to the nearest edge. In the sweep that happened in 803 of the 8,192 scales, close to 1 in 10. In 521, no text reached AA. In 276, one already did and the color moved anyway, because of that margin. The remaining 6 are white and three near-white yellows, which fall outside the range of the lightest step (100 in light mode, 1000 in dark), and the largest shift was 0.029 in OKLCH lightness, under 3 points out of 100; the editor tells you when it happens and by how much. I decided it that way for two reasons, and both come from the rule at the top. One is that accessibility is a principle in Taisho. The other is how much more that principle is worth when it's computed and adjusted for you.

    In a recent development, what I measured is each step's text on that same step. Any two colors from the scale, paired with each other, are outside it.

    The sweep is also a grid of 16 values per channel, not all 16.7 million colors, and I ran it with the default grays: a theme can tint its grays, and that case isn't in these numbers.

    Industry observers note that the rest of this article, before and after this section, describes what the engine does today, with its numbers. This section covers what I found when I rechecked it and what it will do in version 0.17, which I'm already working on. The latest numbers are in the table at the end, next to today's.

    I went back over the warning the generator prints when it shifts a color, and found two things in the engine, plus a third in my own fix.

    According to recent reports, A correction can make things worse. The nearest edge can be step 500's, which sits at 4.2 against the background. Of the 797 scales that get shifted for falling in that zone, 401 go to that edge and end up, once shifted, below 4.5 against the background. In 97 of those 401, measured in 8 bits, the color used to reach it. #767676 in light mode is one of them: measured in 8 bits, it has 4.33:1 with text on it and 4.54:1 against the background, and after the shift it has 4.72 and 4.17. Unshifted, that gray reaches 4.5 against the background and can be used as text on the page. Shifted, it can't: the engine takes away something it had. It repairs one measurement and breaks another I wasn't looking at.

    In a recent development, it also moves colors that don't need it, because of the margin from the previous section. #2563EB in light mode gets 4.62:1 with text on it and 5.17:1 against the background, and it gets shifted anyway.

    It has been revealed that the third isn't in the published engine: it showed up in my fix, while I was working on the other two. The first version compared against the unrounded text gray. For #e22a99 in dark mode it got 4.5000, and what I was calling a pass is 4.48 on the 8 bits per channel the browser paints.

    Sources indicate that in 0.17 the engine measures both ratios, text on the color and the color against the background, and asks 4.5:1 of each. For a starting color that falls between two steps, and for the edge it would move to, it also measures them in 8 bits; the other steps of the scale stay on the computed value. A color between two steps that meets both stays exact. One that fails either gets shifted to the nearest edge that meets both, in whichever direction that is. If you'd rather keep your exact color even when it falls short, say so in the theme with seedFit: { brand: 'keep' }; 'shift' accepts the move. The warning prints both ratios, before and after, and the line to write.

    Industry observers note that the cost is that this edge is usually farther away: fewer colors get shifted, but the ones that do move farther. Among the shifted colors in that zone, the average shift goes from 0.013 to 0.030 in lightness, and the largest from 0.029 to 0.059. #767676 gets 0.019 lighter in OKLCH lightness today and will get 0.037 darker in 0.17. The lowest text contrast drops too, from 4.63 to 4.50, because colors that only just pass are no longer moved. Here's the same sweep, 4,096 colors and 8,192 scales, on today's engine and on 0.17's:.

    The quickest way is the homepage. It has a theme editor with a field where you can type a hex, and the whole page repaints with that color, with each step's text contrast shown. The editor calls the same function the package ships, which applies the theme in the browser without compiling CSS, in a project that already bundles its modules:.

    To use the whole system there are two routes. From a CDN it's three lines of HTML, listed in the installation guide, and nothing to install. With the package, the CSS is compiled with your own colors and fonts:.

    I started this because I didn't want contrast to depend on me remembering to check it on every project. For color, it no longer does: I pick one and the system works out the rest. It's only one part of a design system, but it's the part that convinced me the rule could actually be kept.

    The engine lives in src/lib/theme/palette.ts in the repository, about 350 lines. If a color breaks it, I'd like to see it: open an issue on the repository with the hex and the mode where it fails.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that deploying AI dispatch routing for HVAC and plumbing contractors is frequently pitched as the fastest path to eliminating windshield time and maximizing daily billable technician hours.
    • The failure of algorithmic dispatch in the mechanical trades is not caused by mathematical flaws in routing engines.
    • In a recent development, standard map-routing algorithms treat technicians as interchangeable vehicles carrying uniform packages.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that deploying AI dispatch routing for HVAC and plumbing contractors is frequently pitched as the fastest path to eliminating windshield time and maximizing daily billable technician hours. Commercial field service management platforms claim their algorithms can automate the dispatch whiteboard, recalculating routes dynamically to squeeze two extra service calls into every technician's schedule. Yet, mechanical contractors who flip on default algorithmic dispatch frequently watch their average ticket revenue decline, callback rates spike, and their best senior service technicians threaten to quit.

    The failure of algorithmic dispatch in the mechanical trades is not caused by mathematical flaws in routing engines. It is caused by an objective function mismatch.

    In a recent development, standard map-routing algorithms treat technicians as interchangeable vehicles carrying uniform packages. In residential and commercial mechanical service, technicians are revenue producers with vastly different diagnostic skill sets, sales closing rates, and specialized toolkits. Routing purely for geographical proximity sends the closest technician rather than the most profitable one.

    According to recent reports, for foundational operational strategies, pair this guide with our AI guide for HVAC, plumbing, and electrical contractors, our framework for measuring AI ROI in small business, and our practical guide to building a small business tech stack from scratch. Field software benchmarks are discussed by platforms like BuildOps alongside HVAC contracting resources from the Air Conditioning Contractors of America.

    Modern field service scheduling engines evaluate live dispatch queues through multi-variable constraint satisfaction algorithms.

    Instead of a human dispatcher manually staring at a computerized map and guessing technician arrival times, the software continuously ingests live telemetry, historic job completion data, and incoming customer booking forms:.

    Contractors encounter friction with automated dispatch because mechanical contracting operates in an unpredictable physical environment with severe operational penalties for miscalculation.

    The reality on the ground disrupts theoretical routing models in three distinct areas:.

    When an automated system schedules appointments based on flawed historical data, minor morning delays cascade across the afternoon. A technician delayed by sixty minutes on a frozen evaporator coil causes four subsequent customer appointments to slip, prompting furious inbound phone calls to the office asking: "Where is my technician?".

    The central debate in contractor operations is whether the dispatch algorithm should minimize windshield time or maximize gross profit per technician labor hour.

    Sources indicate that contractors who configure their software to prioritize shortest mileage frequently suffer severe margin compression. Consider this illustrative field comparison (assuming standard residential HVAC equipment, install-crew, and overhead costs on replacement work):.

    Saving twenty-six minutes of windshield time and two gallons of gasoline does not compensate for losing a high-margin diagnostic replacement.

    Many high-performing contracting firms configure weighted objective functions as a starting point (for instance, assigning roughly 70% to 80% of weighting to technician first-time fix rate and replacement diagnostic capability while capping extra drive time at 25 minutes).

    It has been revealed that mechanical service calls are prone to scope creep. A technician dispatched to clear a simple residential kitchen sink trap frequently uncovers a collapsed clay sewer line under the foundation.

    A one-hour scheduled drain clearing quickly turns into a four-hour excavation inspection and camera locating project.

    When an unexpected four-hour scope expansion occurs, a rigid algorithmic scheduler encounters an emergency paradox:.

    To manage scope expansion, contractors must establish a dual-tier dispatch architecture:.

    Morning schedules should feature high-certainty maintenance calls or pre-inspected repairs, while afternoon schedules include designated floating buffer windows.

    Recent findings suggest that during peak summer heatwaves or winter freezes, emergency no-heat and active water-burst calls are held in a dynamic staging bucket. The system alerts the human dispatch supervisor with three recommended redistribution options, requiring human confirmation before customer arrival text messages are altered.

    Sources indicate that field service technicians are notoriously protective of their daily autonomy. When management implements automated dispatch without proper change management, technicians quickly find ways to undermine the system.

    Common methods technicians use to game automated routing software include:.

    To prevent staff rebellion, contractor leadership must establish transparency. Explain to technicians that the software is deployed to eliminate unpaid evening travel and reduce chaotic zig-zag driving across town, rather than to micromanage their breaks. Most importantly, keep human dispatchers in the loop. The software must serve as a recommendation engine that suggests optimal pairings while allowing human dispatchers to lock VIP accounts, protect technician personal commitments, and accommodate field realities.

    Mechanical trade business owners and service operations managers should execute a structured four-phase transition before fully engaging automated dispatch:.

    Audit and standardize invoice codes across historical job tickets. Filter out skewed records where technicians forgot to clock out before lunch, establishing realistic baseline durations for standard furnace repairs, drain cleanings, and water heater swaps.

    It has been revealed that catalog every technician's mechanical certifications (EPA Universal, NATE heat pump, commercial boiler, licensed plumbing contractor) into the scheduling engine. Connect mobile truck inventory feeds to prevent routing technicians to calls requiring unstocked specialized parts.

    In a recent development, configure the dispatch algorithm's objective function to allocate seventy percent weighting to first-time fix rates and replacement sales capability, capping additional drive time at twenty-five minutes. Establish morning anchor jobs and dynamic afternoon emergency buffer slots.

    Run half the service fleet on algorithmic recommendations and half on manual dispatch. Evaluate average ticket size, technician callback rates, fuel consumption, and employee sentiment, preserving human dispatcher veto authority to lock priority accounts.

    Automated dispatch routing offers mechanical contractors practical ways to cut windshield waste and scheduling friction. However, treating residential and commercial service as a pure shortest-distance problem erodes speed-to-lead conversion and job profitability. By prioritizing technician diagnostic skill tags, configuring revenue-weighted dispatch rules, and keeping human dispatcher veto control intact, trade contractors scale field output without losing ticket margins or senior techs.

    • Industry observers note that blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

    It has been revealed that it’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

    Industry observers note that blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

    A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

    Industry observers note that A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

    Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

    Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

    To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:.

    Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

    Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

    It has been revealed that and that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more promptly than ever.

    It has been revealed that even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

    In a recent development, blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

    Sources indicate that although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

    Recent findings suggest that tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

    Sources indicate that blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

    Recent findings suggest that blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

    Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

    Industry observers note that blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

    Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

    Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

    Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

    I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

    Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

    Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of customers constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

    Coinbase Global is at the moment the biggest blockchain organization in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

    Recent findings suggest that blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

    Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency.

    Sources indicate that generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

    It has been revealed that blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain.     Node.js Candidate Search Retrieval Pipeline with 3 Grounded Fallbacks

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For recruiting candidate search, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback.
    • This is a retrieval problem before it is a generation problem.
    • According to recent reports, I use three stages.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For recruiting candidate search, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback. Start with the tenant's private index, broaden only when its evidence is thin, and return document identifiers or URLs beside each claim. A slower, less complete answer is preferable to a fast match that a recruiter cannot audit.

    This is a retrieval problem before it is a generation problem. The flow below keeps candidate records, access-control metadata, and citation fields together; it also gives a web-backed lookup a fixed budget so an unavailable source cannot hold the search screen hostage.

    According to recent reports, I use three stages. Stage one searches the tenant's curated candidate collection with hard filters. Stage two searches a shared, policy-approved talent pool only when the first stage returns too few eligible hits. Stage three performs a web lookup for public portfolio evidence, then marks those results as external and lower-trust. Every stage emits the same result contract, so the caller does not need to know which path answered.

    Sources indicate that the fallback condition is evidence-based, not an exception catch. A result set can be non-empty and still fail a minimum score, freshness, or citation threshold. Conversely, a transient 429 from a web source should consume one retry and then end the stage; it should not silently turn a private search into an unbounded scrape.

    Recent findings suggest that here is a compact TypeScript skeleton. The adapters are deliberately boring: a vector store, a keyword store, and a web search service can be swapped independently. tenantId, ACL labels, and source locators remain mandatory at the boundary.

    In a recent development, the sample uses an intentionally small limit and timeout. Tune them with an evaluation set, not intuition. The vital invariant is that webIndex cannot remove the tenant filter from earlier hits, and an empty external response is still an honest result rather than a fabricated candidate.

    Recent findings suggest that index one candidate profile as several traceable items: employment history, skills, certifications, and portfolio links. Each item keeps a stable evidence.id, its original URL or document key, an patch timestamp, and the access labels needed by the viewer. Store the source text or excerpt alongside the embedding. Rewriting a profile into a summary before indexing makes later review harder because the summary no longer proves what the source mentioned. I also keep the source system's content version and deletion marker, because a recruiter should be able to tell whether a result was current when the query ran. When a candidate changes employers, the old item is not silently overwritten: the newly introduced item receives a new version, the old one is excluded from normal retrieval, and an audit record points to the replacement. That extra bookkeeping feels slow during ingestion, but it prevents a familiar support question: “Why did this answer cite a role the candidate left last year?”.

    Apply authorization twice. Filter at query time, then filter again after merging stages. The second check protects against adapter mistakes and stale ACL metadata. A shared record that lacks a tenant mapping is not a public record; quarantine it from the result set and log the missing field.

    It has been revealed that for generation, pass evidence as numbered passages and require citations in the output schema. The UI should link [3] to the stored locator, not to a URL invented by the model. If no passage supports a claim, return “insufficient evidence” and let the recruiter refine the query.

    Industry observers note that set a deadline per stage and a total deadline for the request. In the example, the total can reach roughly 2.6 seconds before serialization, so production code should reserve headroom for reranking and rendering. Record stage latency, hit count, minimum score, citation count, timeout, and retry status as structured fields. A single aggregate latency metric will hide a web fallback that is quietly consuming the budget.

    Retry only conditions that are plausibly temporary. HTTP 429 deserves a bounded retry and respect for the source's Retry-After guidance when available. A malformed query, a denied tenant, or a 4xx policy response should not be retried. When a stage times out, return the evidence already collected and mark the response as partial so users understand why public results are absent.

    Recent findings suggest that make ingestion idempotent. Derive an item key from tenant, candidate, source locator, and content version; upsert that key and explicitly delete records removed from the source. Otherwise a profile update can leave two stale embeddings, and a fallback may cite the older one. This is an ordinary data-lifecycle issue, but it directly changes ranking quality.

    In a recent development, the catch is that broadening search can change the meaning of “best candidate.” If a job requires verified work authorization or an internal referral, a web fallback is not suitable even when it improves recall. Stick with the private index and return fewer results. If regional residency rules prohibit a shared pool, remove that stage rather than hiding it behind a flag.

    In a recent development, I am not sure one score threshold will transfer across job families: a data-engineering query and a design query have different vocabulary and profile density. Resolve that uncertainty with a labeled set of recruiter queries, measuring recall at a fixed citation requirement and checking false-positive rates by tenant. Keep threshold changes versioned so an evaluation can explain why a candidate moved.

    The right architecture is therefore a policy pipeline, not a list of providers. Keep the internal interface stable, make each fallback observable, and let evidence quality decide when to broaden. Generation can summarize the returned passages later; retrieval must first prove where they came from.

    #23450. Tracking Project Progress with Task Output Quantities
